extracted.intended_audience: theatre directors, producers, costume designers, stage-managers, and students of drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing and mounting stage productions with an emphasis on costume, historical dress (archæology), and the illusionistic effects these choices produce. Advises directors and designers on choosing dates, employing specialists, and using costume to shape character, plot, and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume as a means of producing dramatic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The point … is, not that Shakespeare appreciated the value of lovely costumes in adding picturesqueness to poetry, but that he saw how important costume is as a means of producing certain dramatic effects.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use costume deliberately to create or enhance dramatic effects—make dress expressive of situation and action rather than mere decoration. Examples cited: Measure for Measure, Twelfth Night, Cymbeline, Merry Wives of Windsor—many plots depend on character dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to small details of dress (they can condition action)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Even small details of dress, such as the colour of a major-domo’s stockings, the pattern on a wife’s handkerchief, the sleeve of a young soldier, and a fashionable woman’s bonnets, become in Shakespeare’s hands points of actual dramatic importance, and by some of them the action of the play in question is conditioned absolutely.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to and design minute costume details because they may become plot devices or emotional cues (handkerchiefs, napkins, rings, stained cloths). Small items can trigger revelations or drive scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disguises to transform identity and advance plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous examples: ‘Posthumus hides his passion under a peasant’s garb, and Edgar his pride beneath an idiot’s rags; Portia wears the apparel of a lawyer, and Rosalind is attired in “all points as a man.”’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ disguise and cross-dressing thoughtfully as a dramatic device to change perception, reveal truths, or create irony; ensure costume convincingly conveys the intended transformed identity to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume intensifies dramatic situation and climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: ‘After slaughter of Duncan, Macbeth appears in his night-gown… Timon ends in rags the play he had begun in splendour; … the climax of The Tempest is reached when Prospero, throwing off his enchanter’s robes…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes or contrasts in dress at key moments to signal turning points, reveal inner state, or heighten the emotional or symbolic climax of a scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate costume into dialogue and metaphor (costume in text as stage cue)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In the actual dialogue also some of the most vivid passages are those suggested by costume.’ Examples include Rosalind’s: ‘Dost thou think, though I am caparisoned like a man…’ and Constance’s: ‘Grief fills the place of my absent child, / Stuffs out his vacant garments with his form.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design costumes that the text can reference and that actors can use as tangible emblems in speech and action; allow costume to provide visual metaphors and stage business that enriches lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic use of archæology / historical costume (not pedantry)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘For archæology, being a science, is neither good nor bad, but a fact simply. Its value depends entirely on how it is used, and only an artist can use it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical accuracy where it serves composition and unity; avoid pedantic, piecemeal anachronistic detail that distracts. Archæological detail should be subordinated to artistic effect and the play’s spirit, not shown off for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the date of the drama by its general spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In designing the scenery and costumes for any of Shakespeare’s plays, the first thing the artist has to settle is the best date for the drama. This should be determined by the general spirit of the play, more than by any actual historical references which may occur in it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix the production’s period to suit the play’s mood and themes rather than slavishly following every historical reference; once the date is fixed, use archaeological facts to inform and enrich the visual design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble a skilled production team and specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To put any play of Shakespeare’s on the stage, absolutely as he himself wished it to be done, requires the services of a good property-man, a clever wig-maker, a costumier with a sense of colour and a knowledge of textures, a master of the methods of making-up, a fencing-master, a dancing-master, and an artist to direct personally the whole production.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure technical specialists (props, wigs, costume, make-up, fight and movement coaches, choreography) to realize complex historical or illusionistic stagings accurately and effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid or correct anachronisms where they harm the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It has been said that the anachronisms in the plays themselves show us that Shakespeare was indifferent to historical accuracy… the anachronisms are really few in number, and not very important, and, had Shakespeare’s attention been drawn to them by a brother artist, he would probably have corrected them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize jarring anachronisms that undermine credibility; treat remaining ones as potential blemishes to be fixed by careful mounting unless they serve a deliberate artistic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical accuracy enhances illusion when subordinated to composition
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘For what is the use to the stage of that archæology … but that it, and it alone, can give us the architecture and apparel suitable to the time in which the action of the play passes?’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use period-appropriate architecture and costume to situate action and create a convincing world, but ensure archaeological fidelity serves the play’s unity and compositional aims rather than dominating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual presentation should replace tedious description
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The stage is not merely the meeting-place of all the arts, but is also the return of art to life.… the ancient world wakes from its sleep, and history moves as a pageant before our eyes, without obliging us to have recourse to a dictionary or an encyclopædia for the perfection of our enjoyment.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer vivid, well-designed visual staging that conveys background, atmosphere, and historical detail directly to the audience instead of relying on exposition or didactic lecturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume should express character, social type, and racial identity authentically
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He is even true to the characteristics of race. Hamlet has all the imagination and irresolution of the Northern nations, and the Princess Katharine is as entirely French as the heroine of Divorçons.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design clothing and appearance that reflect a character’s social status, nationality, temperament, and role in the narrative so that costume becomes an immediate index of personality and social meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use costume for irony, contrast, and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘But nobody from the mere details of apparel and adornment has ever drawn such irony of contrast, such immediate and tragic effect, such pity and such pathos, as Shakespeare himself.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit contrasts between dress and circumstance (e.g., rags vs. cloth of gold, funeral dress vs. bridal imagery) to produce irony, deepen emotional resonance, or generate tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a comprehensive and appropriate stage wardrobe and props
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventory evidence: lists of costumes for cardinals, shepherds, kings, clowns, green coats for Robin Hood’s men, helmets, lances, imperial crowns, papal tiaras, etc., showing a desire to give every character an appropriate dress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a full wardrobe and accessory inventory that supplies appropriate attire and props for each role and occasion in the play, enabling the director to realize specific costume-based stage business and historical types.
